new_statements.rule_in_words: Wynne treats Mbukushu as a language with lexical H/L tone patterns (sonogram counts of HL/LH/LL words) and marks tone in the dictionary; beyond tone he notes only an occasional 'slight stress'/prominence on one syllable of low-toned words, whose position and cause he leaves undetermined. No fixed stress position is stated; the only positional hint is that the penultimate vowel of a verb can be lengthened (doubled) for emphasis in imperatives (-terera > tereere).
new_statements.exceptions: High tone may fall on the infinitive prefix ku- (e.g. kúfa 'die'); nasals m/n act as depressors producing rising/falling contours; penultimate vowel doubling for emphasis in imperatives.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms: 'lexical tone is the tone pattern of the word in isolation... not the tone pattern of the word at the end of a statement'; prominence marks are per dictionary entry (word level). Fieldwork among Hambukushu of Ngamiland (Etsha/Shakawe, Botswana) with Namibian and Angolan variants noted.
new_statements.identity_note: Wynne 1978/1980 describes Mbukushu (Thimbukushu, mbuk1240) as spoken by the Hambukushu of Ngamiland, Botswana (Etsha settlement, Shakawe), with Namibian (SWA) and Angolan lexical variants flagged; same language as Fisch's Namibian Thimbukushu, no separate glottocode.
